1.pericope_label: And the king sent, and they gathered unto him all the elders of Judah and of Jerusalem. And the king went up into the house of the Lord, and all the men of Judah and all the inhabitants of Jerusalem with him, and the priests, and the prophets, and all the people, both small and great: and he read in their ears all the words of the book of the covenant which was found in the house of the Lord. And the king stood by a pillar, and made a covenant before the Lord, to walk after the Lord, and to keep his commandments and his testimonies and his statutes with all their heart and all their soul, to perform the words of this covenant that were written in this book. And all the people stood to the covenant.

schools.summary: Ellicott takes the prophets for members of a prophetic order which by then formed a distinct class, and dismisses the Targum's rendering of scribes as naming a class that hardly existed so early. On who read the book he will not commit, allowing it was perhaps the king himself but not necessarily, since what a man does by another he does by himself; he calls the assembly of all the men of Judah a natural hyperbole, the temple court not being able to hold the entire population; and he glosses the pillar as the stand or dais and the people's standing as entering the covenant. Delitzsch suggests Jeremiah and Zedekiah among the prophets and gives Josiah a purpose in summoning them, that they might afterwards press the covenant duties on the people by their preaching. On the reading he answers flatly that he read means he had it read, that duty having devolved on the priests as keepers of the law, and on the people's assent he rejects the reading that they stood firm or continued in the covenant, holding that they entered into it. Both note that Chronicles has Levites in place of the prophets.
Gill notes that the pillar is thought to be the brazen scaffold Solomon made, on which the kings stood, and that Josiah stood there at the reading of the law as Solomon had at the dedication.

Clarke finds the scene singular: the high priest, the scribes, the priests and the prophets are all gathered, and yet the king reads, when it is strange that the high priest or some prophet certainly present did not read the sacred book; he concludes that Josiah considered himself a mediator between God and the people. He renders the pillar as the stairs or pulpit, the brazen scaffold on which the kings were accustomed to stand, and sets out the covenant in two parts, a general undertaking to walk after Jehovah and take his law for the rule of conduct, and a particular one to bend the whole heart and soul to its observance, so that they might not only have religion without but piety within. Wesley offers Jeremiah, Zephaniah and Urijah for the prophets, or the sons of the prophets, repeats Henry almost word for word on the king as reader, and adds that the people possibly declared their consent by standing up as the king had stood.

Henry sets the frame: Josiah had been told the ruin of Jerusalem could not be prevented and that he himself would only be spared the sight of it, yet he did not sit down in despair because he could not do all he would, but would do his duty and leave the event to God. On the reading he takes the king's part as exemplary rather than strange, since Josiah thought it not below him to be a reader any more than Solomon to be a preacher or David a door-keeper in the house of God. From the scene he draws three political conclusions: that parliaments are no diminution to the honour and power of good princes but a great support to them; that it is really the interest of princes to promote the knowledge of the scriptures in their dominions; and that it is no abridgment of the liberty even of princes to be in bonds to God. He adds that it is of good use to oblige ourselves to our duty with all possible solemnity, especially after notorious backslidings, since an honest mind does not shrink from positive engagements.

4.pericope_label: And the king commanded Hilkiah the high priest, and the priests of the second order, and the keepers of the door, to bring forth out of the temple of the Lord all the vessels that were made for Baal, and for the grove, and for all the host of heaven: and he burned them without Jerusalem in the fields of Kidron, and carried the ashes of them unto Beth–el. And he put down the idolatrous priests, whom the kings of Judah had ordained to burn incense in the high places in the cities of Judah, and in the places round about Jerusalem; them also that burned incense unto Baal, to the sun, and to the moon, and to the planets, and to all the host of heaven. And he brought out the grove from the house of the Lord, without Jerusalem, unto the brook Kidron, and burned it at the brook Kidron, and stamped it small to powder, and cast the powder thereof upon the graves of the children of the people. And he brake down the houses of the sodomites, that were by the house of the Lord, where the women wove hangings for the grove. And he brought all the priests out of the cities of Judah, and defiled the high places where the priests had burned incense, from Geba to Beer–sheba, and brake down the high places of the gates that were in the entering in of the gate of Joshua the governor of the city, which were on a man’s left hand at the gate of the city. Nevertheless the priests of the high places came not up to the altar of the Lord in Jerusalem, but they did eat of the unleavened bread among their brethren. And he defiled Topheth, which is in the valley of the children of Hinnom, that no man might make his son or his daughter to pass through the fire to Molech. And he took away the horses that the kings of Judah had given to the sun, at the entering in of the house of the Lord, by the chamber of Nathan–melech the chamberlain, which was in the suburbs, and burned the chariots of the sun with fire. And the altars that were on the top of the upper chamber of Ahaz, which the kings of Judah had made, and the altars which Manasseh had made in the two courts of the house of the Lord, did the king beat down, and brake them down from thence, and cast the dust of them into the brook Kidron. And the high places that were before Jerusalem, which were on the right hand of the mount of corruption, which Solomon the king of Israel had builded for Ashtoreth the abomination of the Zidonians, and for Chemosh the abomination of the Moabites, and for Milcom the abomination of the children of Ammon, did the king defile. And he brake in pieces the images, and cut down the groves, and filled their places with the bones of men.

schools.summary: Ellicott disputes the black derivations of the idolatrous priests' name on a ground nobody else raises, that priests wore white throughout the ancient world except on special occasions, and proposes instead a root meaning to weave, giving weaver of spells, since magic was an invariable concomitant of false worship. On Tophet he offers the burning place, then prefers a modification suggesting a word meaning to spit, so the name itself calls the place an abomination, and adds that Hinnom may mean shrieking. He separates Baal from the sun, following the versions in supplying an and, and rebukes a critic who had called the Hebrew historians superficial for confusing them, since in the Assyrian system they were distinct deities. On the horses of the sun he supplies the classical evidence and argues from the wording that the chariots were burnt where the horses were only taken away, a distinction meaningless had the whole been one work of art in bronze. Delitzsch takes the priests of the second order for the common priests as distinguished from the high priest, and says the Rabbins are wrong in making them vicars of the high priest.

Gill offers for the priests of the second order the second course, or the two chief priests next the high priest from the lines of Eleazar and Ithamar, and the Targum's Sagan, a deputy of the high priest, which is the very explanation Delitzsch rejects.

Clarke says frankly that who the idolatrous priests were is not well known, notes that the Chaldee, Syriac and Arabic call them simply the priests, and derives the name from a root meaning to be scorched or made dark, their business being to attend the fires.

Henry opens with two things he cannot get over: that so many wicked things should have got in and kept standing so long, when Josiah had reigned eighteen years and set the people a good example, and that despite so thorough a riddance Jerusalem was destroyed within a few years, since the generality of the people hated to be reformed. He takes the priests' name as black men, connecting it with the mourning garments of those who sacrificed to Osiris or wept for Tammuz, and derives Tophet from a word for drum, because drums were beaten at the burning of the children so their shrieks might not be heard. On the horses of the sun he marvels that men with the written word among them should conform their religion to the poetical fiction of the sun's chariot, as though the sun needed horses who rejoiceth as a strong man to run a race, when a little philosophy would have shamed them out of it.

15.pericope_label: Moreover the altar that was at Beth–el, and the high place which Jeroboam the son of Nebat, who made Israel to sin, had made, both that altar and the high place he brake down, and burned the high place, and stamped it small to powder, and burned the grove. And as Josiah turned himself, he spied the sepulchres that were there in the mount, and sent, and took the bones out of the sepulchres, and burned them upon the altar, and polluted it, according to the word of the Lord which the man of God proclaimed, who proclaimed these words. Then he said, What title is that that I see? And the men of the city told him, It is the sepulchre of the man of God, which came from Judah, and proclaimed these things that thou hast done against the altar of Beth–el. And he said, Let him alone; let no man move his bones. So they let his bones alone, with the bones of the prophet that came out of Samaria. And all the houses also of the high places that were in the cities of Samaria, which the kings of Israel had made to provoke the Lord to anger, Josiah took away, and did to them according to all the acts that he had done in Beth–el. And he slew all the priests of the high places that were there upon the altars, and burned men’s bones upon them, and returned to Jerusalem. And the king commanded all the people, saying, Keep the passover unto the Lord your God, as it is written in the book of this covenant. Surely there was not holden such a passover from the days of the judges that judged Israel, nor in all the days of the kings of Israel, nor of the kings of Judah; But in the eighteenth year of king Josiah, wherein this passover was holden to the Lord in Jerusalem. Moreover the workers with familiar spirits, and the wizards, and the images, and the idols, and all the abominations that were spied in the land of Judah and in Jerusalem, did Josiah put away, that he might perform the words of the law which were written in the book that Hilkiah the priest found in the house of the Lord.

schools.summary: Ellicott alone asks how a high place of stone could be burnt, wonders whether it was wooden as one critic supposed, and guesses that it resembled a dolmen, of which many hundred have been found in Palestine, with fire kindled under it to crack the slabs so the fragments might be crushed. He notes that no mention is made of the golden bullock, the chief object of worship at Bethel, and takes the silence as indirectly confirming the prophet who foretold it would be carried to Assyria. On the defective account of Josiah turning himself he agrees that words have fallen out and explains how, a transcriber's eye wandering from the first occurrence of the man of God to the second, and places the tombs on the hill-side opposite. On the passover he is exact, that none since the Judges had been celebrated in such strict conformity to the law, and specifies the offerings over and above the paschal lamb and the strict unity of the place; he brushes aside a critic who assumed no passover was ever held before as holding an opinion obsolete even among advanced critics. Delitzsch says Josiah burned the buildings and ground to powder everything of stone or metal, reaches the same conclusion about the calf, and describes the monument as a stone erected on the grave, noting that the reprieve covered the old prophet out of Samaria as well as the man from Judah.

Gill makes the monument a high and large tomb with an inscription, more remarkable than the rest, which caught the king's eye; reports the Jewish tradition that nettles and thistles grew on one side of the grave and sweet herbs on the other, and disowns it at once as not to be depended on; then keeps what he thinks may be right, that the old prophet who asked to be buried with the man of God also ordered a pillar raised over them, which later generations maintained, so the bones of both were saved from the fire. He also contributes the chronology, that Josiah must have begun very early in the year, since all this was done by the fourteenth of Nisan.

Clarke notices that the account of Josiah turning himself is much more complete in the Greek and a Syriac version, and prints what they add, that Jeroboam stood by the altar at the feast and that Josiah, turning about, cast his eyes on the sepulchre of the man of God. On the passover he insists the words apply not to the number present but to the manner and spirit: no passover was kept on purer principles, more heartily joined in, or more religiously observed. Wesley agrees that the golden calf was gone but that Josiah would leave no remains of that idolatry, and alone asks how a king of Judah could act at Bethel at all, supposing the city had long been added to Judah, others having put themselves under her protection after the ten tribes were carried away. On the passover he gives the reasons for its pre-eminence, the solemn care and great preparation and numerous sacrifices, and a joy made greater by the memory of Manasseh and Amon.

25.pericope_label: And like unto him was there no king before him, that turned to the Lord with all his heart, and with all his soul, and with all his might, according to all the law of Moses; neither after him arose there any like him. Notwithstanding the Lord turned not from the fierceness of his great wrath, wherewith his anger was kindled against Judah, because of all the provocations that Manasseh had provoked him withal. And the Lord said, I will remove Judah also out of my sight, as I have removed Israel, and will cast off this city Jerusalem which I have chosen, and the house of which I said, My name shall be there. Now the rest of the acts of Josiah, and all that he did, are they not written in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Judah? In his days Pharaoh–nechoh king of Egypt went up against the king of Assyria to the river Euphrates: and king Josiah went against him; and he slew him at Megiddo, when he had seen him. And his servants carried him in a chariot dead from Megiddo, and brought him to Jerusalem, and buried him in his own sepulchre. And the people of the land took Jehoahaz the son of Josiah, and anointed him, and made him king in his father’s stead.

schools.summary: Ellicott declines to press the difficulty that the same superlative is used of Hezekiah, since a writer would not measure his words by strict proportion in such a case, and adds from the prophet that Josiah's merits did not consist merely in ritual observance, since he is praised for his righteousness as a judge. On the king of Assyria he reopens the usual identification: the assumption that Necho marched against the ruler of what had been the Assyrian empire holds only if Nineveh had already fallen, and on the chronology he prefers it had not, so the king was an Assyrian in the strict sense. He gives Josiah a political motive without moral comment, that he went probably as a vassal of Assyria, resenting a trespass on territory he regarded as his own, and infers from the battlefield that Necho had come by sea and landed at Accho, or Josiah need not have gone so far north. Delitzsch notices that the Hebrew makes a word-play, the Lord turned not answering to the king who turned to the Lord, and names Manasseh as the one whose provocations made the judgment unavoidable.
Gill allows that Hezekiah might excel Josiah in some things and Josiah Hezekiah in others.

Clarke will not rank Josiah below David: perhaps no king since David, and morally considered, David included, none so exemplary in his own conduct or so thoroughly zealous, for David was a greater but not a better man than Josiah. On the unturned wrath he is blunt, that it was of no use to try this fickle and radically depraved people longer and they were respited merely during Josiah's life; he names Nabopolassar as the king in question, and insists that the word used of Josiah at Megiddo is a participle, dying, since he was carried mortally wounded to Jerusalem. Wesley explains the title instead, that the king of Babylon, having rebelled against the Assyrian and then conquered him, is called the Assyrian because he was now head of that empire, and accounts for the unturned wrath from the prophets' complaints and from what happened the moment Josiah was gone.

Henry distributes the superlatives, Hezekiah a nonsuch for faith and dependence upon God in straits and Josiah a nonsuch for sincerity and zeal in a work of reformation. On the wrath he argues backwards from a promise: since the prophet says that if a doomed nation turn from evil God will repent of the punishment, and it was not repented of, the people must never have imbibed Josiah's principles but were turned by force while keeping their affection for their idols. On the war he will not justify the king, who had no clear call and is not found asking counsel of God, and asks what he had to do to act as ally to the king of Assyria; on the promise that he should come to his grave in peace he reports that some think it forfeited, but holds it fulfilled, since Josiah died at peace with God and never saw the destruction, while the providence was still a rebuke to his rashness, for God has promised to keep us in all our ways, but if we go out of our way we throw ourselves out of his protection.

31.pericope_label: Jehoahaz was twenty and three years old when he began to reign; and he reigned three months in Jerusalem. And his mother’s name was Hamutal, the daughter of Jeremiah of Libnah. And he did that which was evil in the sight of the Lord, according to all that his fathers had done. And Pharaoh–nechoh put him in bands at Riblah in the land of Hamath, that he might not reign in Jerusalem; and put the land to a tribute of an hundred talents of silver, and a talent of gold. And Pharaoh–nechoh made Eliakim the son of Josiah king in the room of Josiah his father, and turned his name to Jehoiakim, and took Jehoahaz away: and he came to Egypt, and died there. And Jehoiakim gave the silver and the gold to Pharaoh; but he taxed the land to give the money according to the commandment of Pharaoh: he exacted the silver and the gold of the people of the land, of every one according to his taxation, to give it unto Pharaoh–nechoh. Jehoiakim was twenty and five years old when he began to reign; and he reigned eleven years in Jerusalem. And his mother’s name was Zebudah, the daughter of Pedaiah of Rumah. And he did that which was evil in the sight of the Lord, according to all that his fathers had done.

schools.summary: Delitzsch identifies the significance of the other name given the king by the prophet, to whom it is requited, and uses the prophet's lamentation for the young lion as evidence of character, ascribing to him the disposition of a tyrant given to acts of violence, with Josephus describing him in similar terms; he notes that those who preferred him to his elder brother had set great hopes on his strength and energy against Necho. On the deposition he uses a textual crux to make a point about method: two critics prefer the marginal reading because the Greek supports it in both Kings and Chronicles, but they ought not to appeal to the second passage, since the Greek there does not render the Hebrew of Chronicles but repeats the words already translated in Kings, so the supposed second witness is the first over again. Ellicott had already observed that the people's estimate of the younger son proved fallacious.
Gill identifies this king with the Shallum of the prophet.

Clarke proves from the numbers that the elder son was passed over, since this king was twenty-three and reigned three months while the brother who replaced him was twenty-five, and concludes he was probably raised by the people as of a more active and martial spirit.

Henry adds the motive for the people's choice, that they looked for someone likely to avenge Josiah's death, being more solicitous about that point of honour than about keeping up his reformation, and the issue was accordingly. He observes that the reign was too short for the king's own character to show, so what is recorded is really the character of the patterns he had chosen, and draws the moral that it is of great consequence whom young people choose to imitate. On the tribute he notes the reversal, that formerly the Israelites spoiled the Egyptians and now the Egyptians spoil Israel, and that what made the king poor did not make him good. The change of name draws his sharpest observation: the name the king of Egypt chose has reference to Jehovah, which shows he had no design to make his vassal renounce the religion of his country, and Henry sets against this the king of Babylon, who did not deal so with those whose names he changed. He notices too that the crown of Judah had until now always descended from father to son and never from one brother to another, and closes with the reflection that a little time and slender abilities often suffice to undo the good which pious men have laboured for years to effect, though the good work God begins by his regenerating Spirit cannot be done away.

And Pharaoh–nechoh made Eliakim the son of Josiah king in the room of Josiah his father, and turned his name to Jehoiakim, and took Jehoahaz away: and he came to Egypt, and died there.

And Jehoiakim gave the silver and the gold to Pharaoh; but he taxed the land to give the money according to the commandment of Pharaoh: he exacted the silver and the gold of the people of the land, of every one according to his taxation, to give it unto Pharaoh–nechoh.
Jehoiakim was twenty and five years old when he began to reign; and he reigned eleven years in Jerusalem. And his mother’s name was Zebudah, the daughter of Pedaiah of Rumah.
And he did that which was evil in the sight of the Lord, according to all that his fathers had done.
